faq.a: LDH isoenzymes exist in many tissues; a total serum level reflects the sum of all sources.
No; early injury or diseases that affect other enzymes may have normal LDH.
faq.q: Can a normal LDH rule out serious disease?

faq.a: Rely on clinical pattern and other organ‑specific tests (e.g., troponin, LFTs, smear).
faq.q: What if the laboratory cannot run isoenzyme electrophoresis?

exam: A 28‑year‑old with sickle cell disease presents with severe abdominal pain and LDH 1200 U/L – what is the most likely cause and immediate management? — Consider vaso‑occlusive crisis with hemolysis; give IV fluids, analgesia, and arrange transfusion if Hb falls rapidly.

A patient with fever, cough, and LDH 800 U/L in a rural clinic – how do you differentiate pulmonary infection from malaria‑induced hemolysis? — Order malaria rapid test and chest X‑ray/ultrasound; positive smear points to malaria, infiltrates point to pneumonia.
Why is a high LDH level alone insufficient to diagnose myocardial infarction? — LDH rises later and is non‑specific; troponin provides cardiac‑specific confirmation.

In a child with jaundice, dark urine and LDH 950 U/L, what red‑flag complications must you monitor? — Acute kidney injury from hemoglobinuria and severe anaemia; check renal function and urine output.
How would you interpret a mildly elevated LDH (300 U/L) in a patient on chronic antiretroviral therapy? — May be baseline; assess trend and look for other signs of organ injury before acting.
What is the role of LDH isoenzyme testing in a resource‑limited setting? — Helpful if available to narrow organ source; if not, use clinical clues and other labs.
A patient with known lymphoma shows LDH 1500 U/L after starting chemotherapy – what does this indicate? — Possible tumour lysis; monitor electrolytes, give hydration and allopurinol if available.
When is it appropriate to repeat LDH measurement, and what change would indicate treatment response? — Repeat after 48‑72 h; a falling trend (≥20 % drop) suggests resolution of the acute injury.
ai.title: Increased Lactate Dehydrogenase
ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Elevated LDH reflects cell injury from many common tropical and low‑resource conditions. Interpretation requires linking the pattern to organ sources, clinical context and available tests.

b: LDH is a non‑specific marker of cellular damage.
Levels rise within 6–12 h of injury and peak at 48–72 h.
sections.p: Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) is a cytosolic enzyme present in most tissues. Serum LDH is measured by an enzymatic assay; values above the laboratory upper limit (usually >250 U/L) are considered increased.

b: Mild: usually benign or early disease.
Moderate: warrants focused investigation.
Severe: consider urgent causes such as hemolysis, massive infarction, or disseminated malignancy.
sections.p: There is no universal staging system, but clinicians categorize LDH elevation as mild (250‑500 U/L), moderate (500‑1000 U/L) or severe (>1000 U/L). Higher levels often indicate extensive tissue loss or multi‑organ involvement.

b: Hematologic: hemolytic anemia (sickle cell, malaria, G6PD deficiency), severe malaria, transfusion reactions.
Liver: viral hepatitis B/C, alcoholic hepatitis, hepatic congestion from heart failure.
Cardiac: acute myocardial infarction, myocarditis, pericardial tamponade.
Pulmonary: severe pneumonia, pulmonary embolism, TB pleural effusion.
Renal: acute tubular necrosis, severe dehydration.
Malignancy: lymphoma, Kaposi sarcoma, metastatic carcinoma.
sections.p: In low‑resource East African settings the commonest reasons for LDH rise are grouped by organ system.

b: Fever, jaundice, dark urine → hemolysis.
Chest pain, dyspnoea, diaphoresis → cardiac injury.
Abdominal pain, hepatomegaly, ascites → liver disease.
Weight loss, night sweats, lymphadenopathy → lymphoma.
sections.p: Patients rarely present with LDH alone. The enzyme elevation mirrors the underlying disease, so look for the typical syndrome:

t.b: Which organ is the main source? – Pattern helps differentiate liver (isozyme 5) vs heart (isozyme 1) vs RBC (isozyme 1‑2).

t.a: Complete blood count with peripheral smear
t.b: Is hemolysis present? – Low Hb, high reticulocytes, schistocytes point to RBC destruction.

t.a: Liver function tests (ALT, AST, bilirubin, ALP)
t.b: Is liver injury dominant? – Disproportionate ALT/AST suggests hepatic cause.
Is myocardial injury present? – Positive troponin with high LDH supports cardiac infarction.

t.a: Malaria rapid diagnostic test or thick smear
t.b: Is malaria causing hemolysis? – Positive test confirms parasite‑driven LDH rise.

t.a: Chest X‑ray (or bedside ultrasound if X‑ray unavailable)
t.b: Is there pulmonary infiltrate or effusion? – Helps link LDH to lung pathology.

t.a: HIV test (rapid) and CD4 count if possible
t.b: Is immunosuppression contributing? – HIV‑related lymphoma or opportunistic infections raise LDH.

b: Acute myocardial infarction – risk of arrhythmia, cardiogenic shock.
Severe hemolysis – acute kidney injury from hemoglobinuria.
Massive hepatic necrosis – fulminant liver failure.
Lymphoma with tumour lysis – hyperuricaemia, renal failure.
sections.p: Very high LDH (>1000 U/L) together with organ‑specific signs signals life‑threatening disease.

b: Hemolysis: give antimalarials for malaria, exchange transfusion for severe sickle crisis, avoid oxidant drugs in G6PD deficiency.
Myocardial infarction: aspirin, clopidogrel, anticoagulation, reperfusion (if PCI unavailable, consider thrombolysis).
Viral hepatitis: supportive care, antiviral therapy (e.g., tenofovir for HBV) when available.
Lymphoma: start CHOP‑like regimen if chemotherapy can be accessed; otherwise refer to oncology centre.
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause; LDH itself does not need direct therapy.

b: Monitor renal function and electrolytes in hemolysis.
Vaccinate against hepatitis B, use insecticide‑treated nets to prevent malaria.
Educate on sickle‑cell crisis avoidance (hydration, infection prophylaxis).
sections.p: Repeat LDH after treatment to gauge response; persistent elevation warrants re‑evaluation.

b: AST – also rises in liver and muscle injury; LDH helps differentiate when AST is high but ALT is normal.
CK – specific for muscle breakdown; LDH is broader.
sections.p: Other enzymes that rise with tissue injury can mislead clinicians.

b: Hemolysed blood sample artificially raises LDH – repeat with a fresh tube.
Chronic liver disease may have modest LDH rise despite severe dysfunction.
In malaria endemic areas, low‑grade LDH elevation may be baseline; look for trends.
sections.p: LDH interpretation is limited by several factors.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden chest pain with high LDH and positive troponin – possible MI.
Rapidly falling haemoglobin with dark urine and LDH >1000 U/L – severe hemolysis.
Altered mental status with LDH >1000 U/L and jaundice – fulminant hepatic failure.
